prompt.context: Our client, Tarrant Fixtures, is a low-intensity manufacturing company that produces display fixtures for retail clients. The company's financial performance has deteriorated in each of the last three years. Specifically, they are concerned with the company's falling Return on Investment (ROI).
prompt.question: The CEO has asked us to look into this problem. How can Tarrant Fixtures get back on track?

clarifying_info.q: What types of products does the company produce?
clarifying_info.a: Two types: (1) Custom displays (50% of sales) — produced only when an order is placed and payment is received. (2) Standard displays (50% of sales) — manufactured to open standard sizes/types and stored in inventory (built-to-stock). Five standardized products account for 80% of sales in standardized products; the number of standardized products increased from 5 to 12 over the last 3 years.

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to revenues and costs over the past three years?
clarifying_info.a: Total revenues grew 25%, from $100M to $125M, equally across both product types. Costs of production (COGS, labor, SG&A, etc.) remained stable at 80% of revenue. The company has no new investments in Property, Plant & Equipment (CAPEX = 0).

clarifying_info.q: What has happened to working capital?
clarifying_info.a: Total working capital employed three years ago was $80M; today it is $130M. Inventory levels have increased by 300%, from $25M to $75M, primarily in finished goods.
The market has grown at 25% over the past three years.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's market position?
clarifying_info.a: The client has remained the industry market share leader in displays and has maintained 25% market share over the past three years.
There are several players in the market, but everything has remained stable from a competitive standpoint.

exhibits.title: Working Capital Statement
exhibits.shows: A line-by-line working capital statement showing categories of capital employed (e.g., inventory, accounts receivable, accounts payable, PP&E, cash) for Year 1 and Year 3
exhibits.data: Total Working Capital Year 1: $80M; Total Working Capital Year 3: $130M; Inventory Year 1: $25M; Inventory Year 3: $75M; PP&E, AR, AP, Cash all stable

framework: Define ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed; decompose into numerator (Net Profit) and denominator (Capital Employed)
Analyze Net Profit trend: Revenue growth, cost structure, absolute profit change over three years
Analyze Capital Employed: Break into PP&E and Working Capital; identify which component drove the increase
Deep-dive Working Capital: Examine inventory, AR, AP, cash — identify the root cause of the $50M increase
Identify root causes of inventory build-up: SKU proliferation, demand forecasting errors, obsolete stock
Develop recommendations to reduce inventory and restore ROI

questions.prompt: Walk through the ROI formula and identify the two high-level areas to investigate.
questions.guidance: Candidate must know ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed. Should immediately flag that either profits have fallen or capital employed has risen (or both). A strong candidate frames the entire case around this decomposition before diving in.

questions.prompt: Calculate Net Profit for Year 1 and Year 3. Has profit caused the ROI decline?
questions.guidance: Candidate uses revenue and cost percentages provided. Net Profit = Revenue × (1 - Cost%). Year 1: $100M × 20% = $20M. Year 3: $125M × 20% = $25M. Absolute profit grew 25%, matching revenue growth, so the profit margin is unchanged. Net profit is NOT the cause of the ROI issue.

math.setup: Net Profit = Revenue × (1 - COGS%). Year 1: COGS% = 80%, Revenue = $100M. Year 3: COGS% = 80%, Revenue = $125M.
math.answer: Net profit grew from $20M to $25M (up 25%). Profit is not the cause of ROI decline.

questions.prompt: Analyze Capital Employed. What changed and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should break Capital Employed into PP&E and Working Capital. PP&E: No new CAPEX, so PP&E is unchanged. Working Capital grew from $80M to $130M — a $50M increase. Drilling into working capital, only inventory changed (up $50M, from $25M to $75M). PP&E, AR, AP, and cash are all stable. Inventory is the culprit.

math.setup: Capital Employed = PP&E + Working Capital. Working Capital change = $130M - $80M = $50M. Inventory change = $75M - $25M = $50M.
steps: All other working capital components (AR, AP, Cash) are stable
Therefore, the entire Working Capital increase is attributable to inventory build-up
math.answer: Capital Employed increased by $50M entirely due to inventory growth, from $25M to $75M.

questions.prompt: Calculate ROI for Year 1 and Year 3, and quantify the ROI decline.
questions.guidance: ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed. Year 1: $20M / $80M = 25%. Year 3: $25M / $130M = 19.2%. ROI fell ~5.8 percentage points despite profit growing, because capital employed grew faster than profit.

math.setup: ROI = Net Profit / Capital Employed. Year 1: Net Profit = $20M, Capital Employed = $80M. Year 3: Net Profit = $25M, Capital Employed = $130M.
steps: ROI declined by approximately 5.8 percentage points
math.answer: ROI fell from 25.0% to ~19.2%, driven entirely by the $50M inventory increase, not by profit deterioration.

questions.prompt: What are the likely root causes of the inventory increase?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate will brainstorm structured causes: (1) SKU proliferation — standardized product lines grew from 5 to 12; the top 5 still account for 80% of sales, so the 7 new SKUs add little revenue but require safety stock. (2) Inaccurate demand forecasts — built-to-stock model requires forecasts; errors lead to excess safety stock. (3) Obsolete inventory — older standardized products may be slow-moving or discontinued, sitting in finished goods.

brainstorming.prompt: What can management do to reduce inventory and restore ROI?

categories.name: SKU rationalization
ideas: Reduce standard product line from 12 SKUs back to the top 5 (which drive 80% of standard display sales)
Conduct formal SKU profitability review; discontinue low-volume, low-margin products
Institute a gate process for launching new standard SKUs to prevent future proliferation

categories.name: Demand forecasting improvement
ideas: Invest in demand planning tools and analytics to improve forecast accuracy
Collaborate with key retail clients on demand signals (e.g., point-of-sale data sharing)
Set safety stock levels based on statistically derived demand variability rather than heuristics
Reduce replenishment lead times to lower required safety stock levels

categories.name: Inventory write-down and clean-up
ideas: Write off or actively work down obsolete finished goods inventory (accept short-term P&L hit)
Offer promotions or discounts to sell through slow-moving standard display inventory
Explore salvage or liquidation channels for truly obsolete stock

categories.name: Process and supply chain changes
ideas: Shift more standardized products toward a make-to-order or configure-to-order model where feasible
Implement vendor-managed inventory or consignment arrangements with suppliers to reduce raw material stock
Improve production scheduling to align output more closely with actual orders

recommendation: The client's ROI has fallen from 25% to ~19% over three years due to a $50M increase in inventory (300% growth), not due to any decline in profitability — profits actually grew 25% in line with revenue.
The primary driver is SKU proliferation in the standardized product line (from 5 to 12 SKUs) combined with inaccurate demand forecasting and obsolete stock build-up.

To restore ROI, Tarrant Fixtures should: (1) rationalize the standard product line back to the top 5 SKUs, (2) improve demand forecasting to right-size safety stock, and (3) write off or work down obsolete inventory.
risks: Writing off obsolete inventory will cause an immediate hit to profits, which management may resist
Reducing the SKU count may disappoint some customers or cede niche segments to competitors
Demand forecasting improvements require investment in systems and capabilities and take time to show results
next_steps: Conduct a full SKU profitability analysis to identify candidates for discontinuation
Implement demand planning tools and establish a cross-functional S&OP process
Define a threshold ROI for adding new standard SKUs to prevent future proliferation
Set a timeline for working down or writing off identified obsolete finished goods inventory
